games.title: Reading Detective
games.description: Use unit evidence to solve each reading clue.

rounds.prompt: According to The Speed of a Whisper, what is a rumour, and what are the three reasons the passage gives for why rumours move so fast?
choices: A rumour is a story that runs ahead of its facts, and it moves fast because of excitement, belonging and the sheer speed of modern messages.
She notices that he is filming himself rather than the protest and laughing, and another student tags a post calling it a fake riot for the feed.
She means a story can sound reasonable and still be false, so it must be checked; Amal wants facts before acting, while Nora feels the pull of action.
rounds.answer: A rumour is a story that runs ahead of its facts, and it moves fast because of excitement, belonging and the sheer speed of modern messages.
rounds.explanation: The text opens by calling a rumour "a story that runs ahead of its facts", and then answers "Why do rumours move so fast?" with three reasons: excitement, belonging, and speed itself.

rounds.prompt: At the protest in part 2, what does Amal notice about the boy with the portable speaker, and how does another student label the scene online?
choices: It suggests that one tiny spark can set whole neighbourhoods of conversation alight, and that the fire is far easier to start than to put out.
It advises the reader to pause before sharing -- wait, reread and check -- because strong feelings are exactly the lever a hoax uses to switch off careful thinking.
She notices that he is filming himself rather than the protest and laughing, and another student tags a post calling it a fake riot for the feed.
rounds.answer: She notices that he is filming himself rather than the protest and laughing, and another student tags a post calling it a fake riot for the feed.
rounds.explanation: When Amal scans the crowd, she points out that the boy with the speaker "is filming himself, not the protest" and laughing; then another student tags a post online: "Fake riot for the feed."

rounds.prompt: Why does the toolkit call an anonymous message the weakest kind of source?
choices: A rumour is a story that runs ahead of its facts, and it moves fast because of excitement, belonging and the sheer speed of modern messages.
Because nobody puts their name behind the claim, no one can be questioned or held responsible if it proves false, while an honest organiser signs what they share.
It suggests that one tiny spark can set whole neighbourhoods of conversation alight, and that the fire is far easier to start than to put out.
rounds.answer: Because nobody puts their name behind the claim, no one can be questioned or held responsible if it proves false, while an honest organiser signs what they share.
rounds.explanation: Look at question one of the toolkit: with an anonymous message nobody puts their name behind the claim, so no one can be questioned or held responsible if it proves false, whereas an honest organiser signs what they share.
